newsitem.title: belgium: New allegations hit Belgian troops in Somalia.
newsitem.headline: New allegations hit Belgian troops in Somalia.

text.p: Belgian Defence Minister Jean-Pol Poncelet has reacted in disgust over a new series of pictures purporting to show Belgian paratroops behaving badly while they served with United Nations forces in Somalia in 1993.
"I'm aghast. This is horrible and tasteless," Het Laatste Nieuws newspaper on Wednesday quoted Poncelet as saying.

One of the pictures, published in Wednesday's edition of the paper, showed a soldier urinating on the dead body of a Somali. Another photograph had a soldier with his army boot pressed on the head of a dead Somali.
"Such acts have to be punished severely. There is no room in the army for such people. I will investigate this kind of thing mercilessly," Poncelet said.

An army spokesman said the urinating soldier was bound to be thrown out of the army if he could be identified. But he added that the other pictures -- one showing a Belgian soldier in a Somali's grave- were merely of soldiers in a situation of war.
He noted that placing a foot on the head was not an act of aggression but standard procedure.
Colonel Freddy Van de Weghe, commander Belgium's paratroop brigade, said in a statement the army condemned all racist behaviour and gratuitous violence.
He warned, though, against generalisations and said any isolated cases should not tarnish the army's image as a whole.

"I ask that at the same time people remember that during the 12 months of the (U.N.) "Restore Hope" mission in Somalia the Belgian detachments...were confronted several times with combat situations and that six of their men, including five paratroopers, lost their lives there," the colonel added.
A further 15 had been hurt by bullets and grenades.

A Belgian military court said last week it had arrested one soldier and was investigating others over allegations they tortured children in Somalia following a first series of pictures and stories printed in Het Laatste Nieuws.
Belgian troops serving in Somalia have already been repeatedly accused of human rights abuses.
In August 1993, while they were still in the country, there were allegations they had massively understated the number of Somalis they had killed during military operations.

The allegations, by five of the paratroopers, also said the 1,000 Belgian troops based in Kismayu in southern Somalia often fired at armed Somali fighters even if they themselves had not come under attack.
In October 1995 nine Belgian soldiers accused of maltreating Somali children were acquitted by a Brussels miltary court, and another was given an eight-day suspended jail sentence.
